questions.question: Explain the background to the assassination at Sarajevo.
questions.expected_answer: Austria-Hungary administered Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1878 and annexed it in 1908, angering Serbia and Russia, because many Bosnians were Serbs and Serbian nationalists wanted South Slav unity. Austria-Hungary, a multinational empire, feared Serbian nationalism would break it apart, especially after Serbia grew in the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913. The Black Hand, a secret society of Serbian officers led by Colonel Apis, and the Young Bosnia movement were willing to use violence. Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne, visited Sarajevo on 28 June, the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo.

questions.question: Describe the events of 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo.
questions.expected_answer: Six assassins, organised by Danilo Ilić and armed with help from the Black Hand, waited along the route. Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb that bounced off the archduke's car and exploded under the next car, injuring officers. After a town hall reception, the archduke went to visit the wounded, but his driver followed the original route, turned into Franz Joseph Street and stopped to reverse near Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb, who shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie dead. Princip, too young for execution, was sentenced to twenty years and died in prison in 1918.

questions.question: Explain how the assassination led to a general war in 1914.
questions.expected_answer: Germany gave Austria-Hungary the blank cheque on 5 and 6 July. Austria-Hungary sent Serbia a 48-hour ultimatum on 23 July; Serbia accepted most demands but refused Austro-Hungarian officials investigating on its soil. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Russia mobilised generally on 30 July; Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and France on 3 August and invaded Belgium; Britain, guarantor of Belgian neutrality since 1839, declared war on 4 August, bringing in its empire including South Africa. The assassination was the immediate cause; the long-term causes explain the escalation, in 37 days.
